newsitem.title: USA: U.S. automakers say weak yen hurts domestic sales.
newsitem.headline: U.S. automakers say weak yen hurts domestic sales.

text.p: The U.S. dollar's current strength against the Japanese yen is making it harder for U.S. car manufacturers to compete in the domestic market, the Big Three U.S. automakers and a major union warned in a joint statement on Thursday.
"As new automotive sales figures make clear, the accelerating depreciation of the yen has gone from being a troubling trend to a serious problem," said the statement.
"The yen's continuing fall is translating into more sales for Japanese manufacturers at the expense of U.S. automakers and their American Workers," it added.

Chrysler Corp, Ford Motor Co, General Motors Corp and the United Automobile, Aerospace and Agriculture Implement Workers of America (UAW) issued the statement on Thursday, ahead of this weekend's meeting of finance ministers from the Group of Seven rich industrial countries (G7).

It was the latest in a string of complaints by U.S. automakers and other U.S. manufacturers worried the strong dollar is making their products too costly in global markets. Despite those complaints, the Clinton administration has continued to voice support for a strong dollar.
Recent developments in the currency markets will be discussed by Group of Seven finance ministers at their meeting Saturday in Berlin, Germany, British officials said on Thursday.

The U.S. automakers' statement said the latest data show Japanese manufacturers share of the American auto market rising by 3.3 points to 24.5 percent in January, compared to 21.2 percent a year ago. The share of U.S. manufacturers fell 3.7 points to 71 percent in January, compared to 74.7 percent a year ago, the statement said.

"Since May 1995, the yen's value relative to the U.S. dollar had dropped 38 percent," the statement said. "Recent trade and market statistics clearly indicate that the undervalued yen is putting U.S. automakers at a growing disadvantage to their Japanese competitors, in both the U.S. and Japanese markets."

The statement said that Japanese auto exports to the United States rose sharply in the past six months. It added the weak yen has made it more difficult for U.S. manufacturers to export to the Japanese market because it makes U.S. products more expensive when priced in the weaker Japanese currency.
